title_original: Planches Contact Festival 2026 : Photography Through Generations
excerpt_original: The 17th edition of Planches Contact festival in Deauville investigates the theme of ‘Generations’. Cet article Planches Contact Festival 2026 : Photography Through Generations est apparu en premier sur The Eye of Photography Magazine .

blocks.text: Until January 3, 2027, Deauville is transformed by photography for the 17th edition of the Planches Contact Festival. Les Franciscaines, Le Point de Vue and the beach become spaces for artistic expression around the theme of “Generations”.

“The show is about to begin,” announces Philippe Augier, Mayor of Deauville and Director of Les Franciscaines, as he opens the 17th edition of the Planches Contact Festival. This year, twenty photographers explored the theme of “Generations” during two-month residencies in Normandy, with one residency taking place abroad, in Iran. “The theme came to us when we rediscovered the Generation X project, undertaken by the founders of Magnum Photos in the 1950s,” explains Lionel Charrier, co-artistic director of the festival.

Presented as part of the festival, Generation X brings together the work of eleven photographers, including Henri Cartier-Bresson, David Seymour and Eve Arnold, who documented the lives of the postwar generation around the world. Following in their footsteps, contemporary Magnum photographers, including the agency’s former president Cristina de Middel, extend the project by turning their attention to Generation Z in the countryside and small towns of Normandy.
Generations of photographers

At the heart of Les Franciscaines, the festival opens with an exhibition by Newsha Tavakolian, who was invited to undertake a residency abroad in Tehran, Iran. This is the festival’s second residency outside Normandy, following an initial project in Beirut in 2025. A large yellow-dominated print draws visitors closer. “It’s a photograph of my father, which I then painted yellow,” the artist explains.

In her family, three generations share the same passion for photography. At the age of thirty, Newsha Tavakolian inherited forty-six glass plates from her great-uncle, an Iranian nobleman. The artist brings these archives into dialogue with family photographs taken by her grandfather, who had received a camera from either the French or German embassy, as well as with her own images of contemporary Iran. Through these three photographic collections, intimate and political fragments of her country’s history emerge.

Similarly, the works of Alain and Léo Keler enter into dialogue. Father and son were invited to produce work in Normandy. “It was a pleasure to come here with my father, with whom I have already worked on family-related subjects,” says Léo Keler. Although their approaches differ, a common theme emerges from their images: transmission between generations.

For the past five years, the younger photographer has been documenting social divisions in France. For this residency, he immersed himself in the cahiers de doléances , the notebooks of grievances compiled by the Yellow Vest movement in Normandy. “I managed to obtain the collection and contact a hundred people. Between ten and fifteen responded positively,” he explains. Large-format photographs taken with a view camera are displayed alongside excerpts from these texts, revealing the political and personal dimensions of the demands expressed.

Opposite, Alain Keler chose to revisit his teenage memories, when he was a boarder at the Lycée Albert-Sorel in Honfleur between 1961 and 1964. With emotion, he recounts this period of newfound independence through photographs. “I had someone who acted as my guardian, a friend’s mother, who signed my papers. We used to go clubbing in Deauville. We enjoyed our youth. I hitchhiked home to my parents so I could keep the money intended for the train,” he recalls.
Today, he once again walks the streets of his youth, now transformed. The school has closed, and the local café is no longer a café. But some of his former classmates still live in Honfleur.
Family histories

The photographers form connections with one another, but they also explore their own family histories. With The Sorrowful and Immaculate Heart of Mary , Ed Alcock investigates the people who raised his grandmother, Mary.

“In my family, the story was that she had been adopted by an elderly gentleman in Cowes, on the Isle of Wight — coincidentally, Deauville’s twin town — who had given her a middle-class upbringing. When he died, she was supposedly sent back to her working-class family in northern England,” he explains.

Intrigued by this account, he questioned his parents. His mother then took him to Mary’s house and uncovered a small box concealed inside a French-English dictionary, containing traces of a story very different from the one passed down orally.

As he examined the archives, Ed Alcock discovered two women who appeared to be deeply in love: Florence, his great-aunt, and a mysterious “Mademoiselle”. “The more I look through the letters, the more I discover that it was two women who raised my grandmother, not the elderly gentleman at all,” the artist adds.

From the Isle of Wight to the Normandy coast, the photographer continues his investigation, gathering testimonies and photographing female couples or figures who might embody Mademoiselle. Between intimate archives and collective memory, his work questions the bonds that constitute a family, beyond official narratives and social conventions.
Forging connections
A short distance from Les Franciscaines, near the beach, Sylvie Bonnot, one of the four recipients of a grant from the Photo4Food Foundation, presents a body of work with a striking material quality.

Her project La Concordance des liens has its roots in research conducted in French Guiana, where climbing vines already embodied the notion of connection. Here, the idea takes shape through ropes and garages , metal traps used to harvest shellfish.

The artist joined four fishermen aboard their boat. “On the boat, fishing itself is not what matters most, but the bonds shared by these men, and the experience of witnessing what connects them so deeply,” she explains.

Sylvie Bonnot makes these connections tangible through a process she invented, known as mue (shedding), which involves peeling away the silver-based emulsion from her photographic prints. Applied directly to the wall, these organic forms invite touch, while others, more sculptural, evoke the cliffs of the region. “These shifts and expansions of form express the elasticity of these bonds,” she says.

The festival concludes with its feet in the sand. On the beach, large cubes house the works of Tina Merandon and Claire Adelfang, alongside an extensive retrospective devoted to the New York years of Magnum photographer Bruce Gilden. Between sky, sea and land, the exhibitions continue a shared exploration of the region. The circle is complete.
